questions.q: Which class of adverse drug reactions (ADRs) is predictable from the known pharmacology of the drug, dose-dependent, and accounts for the vast majority of ADRs?
questions.explain: Type A (augmented) reactions are extensions of a drug's primary or secondary pharmacological actions (such as bradycardia with beta-blockers or bleeding with warfarin), making them predictable and dose-related.

open.q: Name the adverse drug reaction class that is dose-dependent, predictable from pharmacology, and most common in clinical practice.

questions.q: Which class of adverse drug reactions is unrelated to the drug's known pharmacology, unpredictable, dose-independent within therapeutic ranges, and often immunologically or genetically mediated?
questions.explain: Type B (bizarre or idiosyncratic) reactions—such as penicillin anaphylaxis, halothane-induced malignant hyperthermia, or G6PD haemolysis—cannot be predicted from normal pharmacological effects and require drug cessation.

open.q: Identify the class of adverse drug reactions that is bizarre, unpredictable from normal pharmacology, and largely dose-independent.

questions.q: Which class of adverse drug reactions results from cumulative, prolonged, or continuous exposure to a drug over months or years?
questions.explain: Type C (chronic or continuous) reactions arise from cumulative exposure, such as analgesic nephropathy from chronic NSAIDs, osteonecrosis of the jaw from bisphosphonates, or adrenal suppression from long-term corticosteroids.

open.q: Name the adverse drug reaction category associated with prolonged or cumulative drug exposure over time.

questions.q: Which class of adverse drug reactions manifests long after drug exposure has ceased, including teratogenesis and drug-induced carcinogenesis?
questions.explain: Type D (delayed) reactions appear well after the drug is discontinued, such as vaginal clear-cell adenocarcinoma years after in utero diethylstilbestrol exposure or secondary leukaemia after alkylating agents.

open.q: Which ADR classification includes teratogenicity and carcinogenesis appearing long after drug discontinuation?

questions.q: Which class of adverse drug reactions occurs shortly after abrupt withdrawal or cessation of a drug, such as rebound hypertension after clonidine discontinuation?
questions.explain: Type E (end-of-use) reactions happen upon stopping a drug abruptly, including opioid withdrawal, benzodiazepine rebound anxiety/seizures, and beta-blocker rebound angina.

open.q: Name the ADR class that occurs upon stopping a medication abruptly, such as rebound hypertension or withdrawal syndrome.

questions.q: Which class of adverse drug reactions represents unexpected therapeutic failure, commonly caused by drug interactions or resistance?
questions.explain: Type F (failure) reactions reflect unexpectedly reduced efficacy—for example, oral contraceptive failure when co-administered with rifampicin or antimicrobial resistance.

open.q: Which ADR classification refers to unexpected failure of treatment efficacy, often due to drug interactions or resistance?

questions.q: A 19-year-old man with glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency develops acute intravascular haemolysis, haemoglobinuria, and jaundice after taking primaquine or dapsone. Why does this occur?
options: Primaquine directly inhibits bone marrow erythropoietin receptors
Deficient G6PD impairs NADPH generation needed to keep glutathione reduced, leaving red cells vulnerable to oxidative damage
Primaquine triggers an IgE-mediated Type I anaphylactic reaction against reticulocytes
G6PD deficiency blocks hepatic glucuronidation of bilirubin
questions.explain: G6PD is the rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway in erythrocytes; without adequate NADPH and reduced glutathione (GSH), oxidative drugs cause haemoglobin denaturation (Heinz bodies) and haemolysis.

open.q: Explain the biochemical mechanism behind drug-induced haemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency.
accept: impaired NADPH generation reduces glutathione leaving red blood cells susceptible to oxidative stress
inability to maintain reduced glutathione against oxidant drugs

questions.q: Which of the following drugs is classically associated with precipitating acute haemolytic anaemia in individuals with G6PD deficiency?
questions.explain: Oxidant agents such as primaquine, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, rasburicase, and certain sulfonamides/fluoroquinolones can trigger haemolysis in G6PD-deficient individuals.

open.q: Name two drugs that can trigger haemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency.

questions.q: Which pharmacogenetic disorder presents with generalized muscle rigidity, high fever, metabolic acidosis, and hyperkalaemia shortly after exposure to succinylcholine or volatile anesthetics like halothane, and is treated with dantrolene?
questions.explain: Malignant hyperthermia is an autosomal dominant pharmacogenetic disorder (most often RYR1 ryanodine receptor mutations) causing excessive Ca2+ release from sarcoplasmic reticulum; dantrolene blocks ryanodine receptors to stop Ca2+ release.

open.q: Name the life-threatening pharmacogenetic anesthetic emergency treated with dantrolene.

questions.q: How does dantrolene act to reverse malignant hyperthermia?
options: By blocking ryanodine receptors (RYR1) on the sarcoplasmic reticulum to inhibit excessive Ca2+ release into skeletal muscle
By acting as a competitive antagonist at neuromuscular nicotinic receptors
By chelating extracellular calcium in systemic plasma
By accelerating renal excretion of volatile anesthetics
questions.explain: Dantrolene binds to ryanodine receptor channels on the sarcoplasmic reticulum of skeletal muscle, halting pathological Ca2+ efflux, hypermetabolism, and rigidity.

open.q: State the mechanism of action of dantrolene in treating malignant hyperthermia.
accept: blocks ryanodine receptors to inhibit calcium release from sarcoplasmic reticulum
inhibits sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium release via ryanodine receptor blockade

questions.q: Which enzyme deficiency causes severe, potentially fatal myelosuppression (neutropenia) when standard doses of azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine are given?
questions.explain: TPMT methylates and inactivates mercaptopurine metabolites; TPMT deficiency diverts purine analogues toward cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides in bone marrow.

open.q: Name the enzyme whose genetic deficiency leads to severe bone marrow toxicity from azathioprine or mercaptopurine.

questions.q: Which enzyme deficiency is linked to severe, life-threatening fluorouracil (5-FU) or capecitabine toxicity (mucositis, myelosuppression, neurotoxicity)?
questions.explain: Over 80% of administered 5-fluorouracil is catabolized by DPD; partial or complete DPD deficiency causes marked accumulation of 5-FU and severe cytotoxic toxicity.

open.q: Identify the enzyme deficiency that predisposes patients to severe fluorouracil toxicity.

questions.q: Why does codeine fail to provide adequate analgesia in individuals who are CYP2D6 poor metabolizers, whereas CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers risk opioid toxicity and respiratory depression even at standard doses?
options: CYP2D6 converts codeine into inactive glucuronides
CYP2D6 is required to pump codeine across the blood-brain barrier
CYP2D6 is the sole enzyme that excretes codeine in bile
CYP2D6 O-demethylates codeine (a weak prodrug) into morphine, which has much higher mu-opioid affinity
questions.explain: Codeine relies on CYP2D6-mediated O-demethylation to form morphine; poor metabolizers get little morphine, while ultrarapid metabolizers convert excessive amounts rapidly.

open.q: Explain why CYP2D6 genetic variants alter both the efficacy and toxicity of codeine.
accept: CYP2D6 converts codeine into active morphine so poor metabolizers lack analgesia and ultrarapid metabolizers risk morphine toxicity
CYP2D6 controls bioactivation of codeine to morphine

questions.q: Why do most low-molecular-weight drugs (haptens) require binding to host proteins before triggering a true immune-mediated drug allergy?
options: Small molecules alone are generally too small to be recognized effectively as immunogens unless conjugated to carrier proteins to form a complete antigen
Host proteins convert all drugs into IgA antibodies
Unbound small drugs are destroyed before reaching lymph nodes
Haptens only bind to erythrocytes without activating lymphocytes
questions.explain: Most drugs or their reactive metabolites act as haptens that bind covalently to host macromolecules (proteins), creating a hapten-carrier complex capable of stimulating an immune response.

open.q: Why do most low-molecular-weight drugs act as haptens that must bind to host proteins to elicit an allergic reaction?
accept: small molecules need a protein carrier to become immunogenic and form a complete antigen
hapten-carrier complex is required to stimulate the immune system

questions.q: Which Gell and Coombs hypersensitivity mechanism mediates acute anaphylaxis, urticaria, and bronchospasm following penicillin administration?
questions.explain: Type I hypersensitivity involves drug-specific IgE bound to tissue mast cells and blood basophils; re-exposure cross-links IgE and triggers release of histamine, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins.

open.q: Which hypersensitivity type underlies acute IgE-mediated drug anaphylaxis and urticaria?

questions.q: Which Gell and Coombs hypersensitivity mechanism causes drug-induced haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, or agranulocytosis via IgG/IgM antibodies directed against drug-modified cell surfaces?
questions.explain: Type II reactions involve IgG or IgM binding to drug-coated blood cells or haptens on cell membranes, causing complement-mediated lysis or phagocytosis by reticuloendothelial macrophages.

open.q: Name the hypersensitivity mechanism responsible for drug-induced immune haemolytic anaemia or thrombocytopenia.

questions.q: Which Gell and Coombs hypersensitivity mechanism causes serum sickness (fever, arthralgia, urticaria, lymphadenopathy, glomerulonephritis) due to circulating antigen-antibody complexes?
questions.explain: Type III reactions result from deposition of soluble drug-antibody immune complexes in small blood vessels and glomeruli, activating complement and recruiting neutrophils.

open.q: Which hypersensitivity type causes drug-induced serum sickness via immune complex deposition?

questions.q: Which Gell and Coombs hypersensitivity mechanism mediates allergic contact dermatitis appearing 24 to 72 hours after topical drug exposure?
questions.explain: Type IV reactions are mediated by sensitized T lymphocytes (CD4+ or CD8+) rather than antibodies, typically developing over 1 to 3 days (e.g., topical neomycin or local anesthetic contact dermatitis).

open.q: Identify the T-cell-mediated delayed hypersensitivity type responsible for allergic contact dermatitis.

questions.q: A 26-year-old patient develops sudden laryngeal stridor, wheezing, generalized urticaria, and hypotension (BP 70/40 mmHg) 10 minutes after receiving intramuscular ceftriaxone. Which drug is the immediate first-line lifesaving treatment?
options: Intramuscular adrenaline (epinephrine) into the anterolateral thigh
questions.explain: Intramuscular adrenaline (1:1000, typically 0.5 mg in adults) is first-line in anaphylaxis: alpha-1 agonism reverses hypotension and mucosal oedema, while beta-2 agonism causes bronchodilation and inhibits mast-cell mediator release.

open.q: Name the immediate first-line drug of choice for acute systemic anaphylaxis.

questions.q: Why are corticosteroids and H1 antihistamines considered adjunctive rather than first-line monotherapy for acute anaphylaxis?
options: They cause severe coronary vasoconstriction and worsen shock
They directly block IgE synthesis within 30 seconds
They replace the need for airway support and oxygen
Their onset of action is too slow to rapidly reverse life-threatening bronchospasm and hypotension compared with adrenaline
questions.explain: Antihistamines and corticosteroids do not rapidly reverse severe bronchoconstriction or cardiovascular collapse; corticosteroids take hours to reduce late-phase inflammation and prevent biphasic relapse.

open.q: Explain why antihistamines and corticosteroids do not replace adrenaline as initial therapy in anaphylaxis.
accept: too slow in onset to rapidly reverse shock and bronchospasm
lack immediate hemodynamic and bronchodilator reversal of life-threatening anaphylaxis

questions.q: During which developmental period of pregnancy is the human fetus most vulnerable to structural congenital malformations (teratogenesis)?
options: The embryonic period of organogenesis (approximately weeks 3 to 8 of gestation)
The third trimester after 32 weeks of gestation
questions.explain: Organogenesis occurs mainly between the 3rd and 8th weeks post-conception (weeks 5 to 10 by LMP), when rapid organ differentiation makes the embryo most susceptible to structural teratogens; third-trimester exposure affects growth and functional maturation.

open.q: Which period of pregnancy carries the highest risk of drug-induced structural birth defects (teratogenesis)?

questions.q: Which classic teratogen taken in early pregnancy caused phocomelia (limb reduction deformities) and congenital anomalies in the mid-20th century?
questions.explain: Thalidomide taken between days 20 and 36 after fertilization caused characteristic limb defects (phocomelia/amelia) and ear/cranial abnormalities, prompting modern teratogenicity testing.

open.q: Name the sedative-antiemetic drug famous for causing phocomelia when taken during early pregnancy.

questions.q: Which antiepileptic drug is strongly associated with neural tube defects (such as spina bifida), developmental delay, and major congenital malformations when used in pregnancy?
questions.explain: Valproate carries a high risk of neural tube defects (~1% to 5%) and neurodevelopmental impairment in children exposed in utero, so it is avoided in women of childbearing potential whenever effective alternatives exist.

open.q: Identify the antiepileptic drug strongly linked to neural tube defects and neurodevelopmental harm in pregnancy.

questions.q: Which class of antihypertensive drugs is contraindicated throughout pregnancy because it causes fetal renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia, and neonatal renal failure?
options: ACE inhibitors (such as enalapril and lisinopril) and ARBs
questions.explain: Inhibiting the renin-angiotensin system lowers fetal renal perfusion pressure and impairs nephrogenesis, leading to oligohydramnios, limb contractures, pulmonary hypoplasia, and fetal/neonatal death.

open.q: Name the antihypertensive drug class contraindicated in pregnancy due to fetal renal failure and oligohydramnios.
accept: angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers

questions.q: Why are tetracyclines avoided in pregnant women and children under 8 years of age?
options: They bind calcium in developing teeth and bones, causing permanent tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia, and risk maternal hepatotoxicity
They cause permanent sensorineural deafness by damaging cranial nerve VIII
They inhibit fetal thyroid hormone synthesis causing cretinism
They trigger acute haemolysis in all fetuses
questions.explain: Tetracyclines chelate calcium in mineralizing tissues, staining deciduous/permanent teeth yellow-brown and inhibiting bone growth; high IV doses in pregnancy can also cause acute fatty liver of pregnancy.

open.q: State the main dental and skeletal adverse effect of tetracyclines in children and fetuses.
accept: permanent tooth discoloration and enamel hypoplasia or inhibition of bone growth
staining of teeth and deposition in bone and teeth

questions.q: Which anti-acne retinoid is a potent human teratogen requiring strict pregnancy prevention before, during, and after treatment?
questions.explain: Systemic retinoids (isotretinoin, acitretin) cause severe craniofacial, cardiac, thymic, and CNS malformations and require strict contraceptive precautions.

open.q: Name the systemic retinoid used for severe acne that is a well-known human teratogen.

questions.q: Which antimicrobial class is characteristically associated with concentration-dependent ototoxicity (vestibular or cochlear damage) and nephrotoxicity?
questions.explain: Aminoglycosides accumulate in inner-ear endolymph/perilymph hair cells and renal proximal tubular cells, causing irreversible hearing loss, vestibular dysfunction, and acute tubular injury.

open.q: Which antibiotic group causes both ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity?

questions.q: Which antituberculosis drug classically causes retrobulbar optic neuritis, manifesting as reduced visual acuity and loss of red-green colour discrimination?
questions.explain: Ethambutol can cause dose-dependent optic neuritis with blurred vision, central scotoma, and red-green colour blindness, which may become irreversible if not stopped promptly.

open.q: Name the antituberculosis drug associated with optic neuritis and red-green colour vision loss.

questions.q: Which antituberculosis drug causes peripheral neuropathy by interfering with pyridoxine (vitamin B6) metabolism, and can be prevented by co-administering pyridoxine?
questions.explain: Isoniazid promotes urinary excretion and inactivation of pyridoxine (vitamin B6), leading to paraesthesias and peripheral neuropathy, especially in slow acetylators, malnourished patients, or HIV.

open.q: Name the antituberculosis drug that causes peripheral neuropathy preventable by vitamin B6 (pyridoxine).

questions.q: Which anticancer drug class is famous for causing cumulative, dose-dependent cardiotoxicity (dilated cardiomyopathy and heart failure) mediated by free-radical myocardial injury?
questions.explain: Anthracyclines generate reactive oxygen species and iron-mediated lipid peroxidation in cardiomyocytes, limiting lifetime cumulative dosing and sometimes warranting dexrazoxane cardioprotection.

open.q: Which class of cytotoxic anticancer drugs causes cumulative dose-related cardiomyopathy?

questions.q: Which cytotoxic alkylating agent causes haemorrhagic cystitis due to its urinary metabolite acrolein, and is prevented using mesna and hydration?
questions.explain: Acrolein irritates the urothelium, causing sterile haemorrhagic cystitis; mesna (2-mercaptoethanesulfonate) binds acrolein in the bladder lumen to form a non-toxic thioether.

open.q: Name the anticancer drug whose metabolite acrolein causes haemorrhagic cystitis, prevented by mesna.

questions.q: Which antitumour antibiotic causes dose-related pulmonary fibrosis and pneumonitis while causing minimal bone marrow suppression?
questions.explain: Bleomycin generates free radicals in lung tissue (which lacks high bleomycin hydrolase activity), risking pulmonary fibrosis; high inspired oxygen concentrations can worsen lung injury.

open.q: Name the cytotoxic agent classically associated with pulmonary fibrosis and minimal myelosuppression.

questions.q: Which drug-induced movement disorder syndrome is characterized by involuntary, repetitive, purposeless choreoathetoid movements of the tongue, lips, and face ('fly-catching' or chewing motions) after prolonged dopamine D2 receptor blockade?
questions.explain: Tardive dyskinesia develops after months or years of typical antipsychotic therapy, likely due to striatal dopamine D2 receptor upregulation/supersensitivity, and often responds poorly to anticholinergics.

open.q: Name the late-onset involuntary orofacial and limb movement disorder associated with chronic antipsychotic exposure.

questions.q: A 24-year-old man started on haloperidol develops severe generalized 'lead-pipe' muscle rigidity, hyperthermia (40.5 C), autonomic instability (tachycardia, labile BP), altered consciousness, and markedly elevated creatine kinase. What is the diagnosis?
questions.explain: NMS is an idiosyncratic, life-threatening reaction to dopamine antagonists characterized by severe muscular rigidity, hyperpyrexia, autonomic instability, and elevated CK; treated with drug cessation, supportive care, dantrolene, and bromocriptine.

open.q: Identify the syndrome of rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, and high creatine kinase caused by dopamine receptor blockade.

questions.q: A patient taking an SSRI is inadvertently prescribed linezolid or a monoamine oxidase inhibitor and presents within hours with agitation, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hyperreflexia, and inducible clonus. Which condition is most likely?
questions.explain: Excessive central and peripheral serotonergic activity produces neuromuscular hyperactivity (clonus, hyperreflexia), autonomic hyperactivity, and mental status changes; cyproheptadine (a 5-HT2A antagonist) may be used in moderate-to-severe cases.

open.q: Name the drug interaction syndrome marked by clonus, hyperreflexia, agitation, and autonomic hyperactivity from excessive 5-HT activity.

questions.q: Which group of drugs can precipitate drug-induced lupus erythematosus (DILE), typically characterized by antinuclear antibodies and antihistone antibodies while sparing severe renal and CNS involvement?
questions.explain: Drug-induced lupus is associated with hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid, quinidine, and minocycline; symptoms usually resolve after stopping the offending drug.

open.q: Name two drugs classically associated with drug-induced lupus erythematosus.

questions.q: Which drug is notorious for causing pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction (hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism), corneal microdeposits, and bluish-grey skin pigmentation during long-term use?
questions.explain: Amiodarone is a lipophilic Class III antiarrhythmic with a very long half-life that accumulates in lung, thyroid, cornea, and skin, requiring baseline and periodic pulmonary, thyroid, and liver monitoring.

open.q: Name the antiarrhythmic drug associated with pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction, corneal deposits, and skin discoloration.

questions.q: Which serious cutaneous adverse drug reaction is characterized by widespread epidermal detachment (>30% body surface area), mucosal erosions, and a positive Nikolsky sign?
questions.explain: TEN (and Stevens-Johnson syndrome, involving <10% BSA detachment) is a severe mucocutaneous drug reaction requiring immediate withdrawal of the culprit drug and burn-unit-level supportive care.

open.q: Name the severe mucocutaneous drug reaction involving widespread epidermal detachment over 30% of body surface area.

questions.q: What is a 'pharmacokinetic' drug interaction?
options: Two drugs acting at the same receptor to block each other's signaling
Two drugs causing additive central nervous system depression
One drug altering the absorption, distribution, metabolism, or excretion (ADME) of another drug
Chemical inactivation of a drug inside an infusion bottle
questions.explain: Pharmacokinetic interactions modify the concentration-time profile (ADME) of a drug at its site of action without directly changing the target tissue's sensitivity.

open.q: Define a pharmacokinetic drug interaction.
accept: one drug alters the absorption distribution metabolism or excretion of another drug
modification of ADME of one drug by another

questions.q: What is a 'pharmacodynamic' drug interaction?
options: Inhibition of hepatic cytochrome P450 by an azole antifungal
Displacement of a drug from plasma albumin
Reduction of gastric absorption by a metal chelate
One drug modifying the pharmacological effect of another drug at the receptor, second-messenger, or physiological level without altering its plasma concentration
questions.explain: Pharmacodynamic interactions involve additive, synergistic, or antagonistic effects on target tissues—for example, alcohol plus benzodiazepines causing additive CNS depression or NSAIDs plus ACE inhibitors impairing renal perfusion.

open.q: Define a pharmacodynamic drug interaction.
accept: one drug modifies the physiological or receptor effect of another without changing its concentration
interaction at the site of drug action altering response

questions.q: Why does combining a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) with an ACE inhibitor or loop diuretic increase the risk of acute kidney injury in a volume-depleted or elderly patient?
options: NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin synthesis (PGE2/PGI2), constricting the afferent arteriole while ACE inhibitors dilate the efferent arteriole, reducing glomerular filtration pressure
ACE inhibitors convert NSAIDs into nephrotoxic oxalates
NSAIDs block aldosterone receptors in the collecting duct
ACE inhibitors cause direct crystallization of NSAIDs in renal tubules
questions.explain: Glomerular filtration relies on prostaglandins maintaining afferent arteriolar patency and angiotensin II maintaining efferent arteriolar tone; blocking both (especially with diuretic volume depletion) sharply lowers GFR.

open.q: Explain the hemodynamic mechanism by which NSAIDs can precipitate acute renal failure in patients taking ACE inhibitors.
accept: prostaglandin inhibition constricts afferent arteriole while ACE inhibition dilates efferent arteriole lowering GFR
loss of prostaglandin-mediated afferent dilation combined with efferent dilation

questions.q: Which combination of drugs carries a high risk of life-threatening hyperkalaemia due to additive potassium retention?
options: ACE inhibitor + potassium-sparing diuretic (such as spironolactone or amiloride)
questions.explain: ACE inhibitors lower aldosterone (reducing distal K+ secretion), while spironolactone antagonizes mineralocorticoid receptors or amiloride blocks ENaC; together they can cause severe hyperkalaemia.

open.q: Which drug combination increases the risk of hyperkalaemia by impairing renal potassium excretion?
accept: ACE inhibitor or ARB with spironolactone

questions.q: Why should patients taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) avoid tyramine-rich foods such as aged cheese, cured meats, and fermented yeast products?
options: Tyramine directly inhibits cholinesterase in the gastrointestinal tract
MAOI therapy causes severe hypoglycaemia when tyramine is eaten
Inhibition of MAO prevents breakdown of dietary tyramine in the gut and liver, allowing tyramine to enter systemic circulation and displace noradrenaline, risking a hypertensive crisis
Tyramine precipitates calcium stones in the renal pelvis
questions.explain: Normally, MAO in the gut wall and liver metabolizes ingested tyramine; when MAO is inhibited, absorbed tyramine enters adrenergic neurons and triggers massive noradrenaline release ('cheese effect').

open.q: Explain why tyramine-rich foods can trigger a hypertensive crisis in patients taking MAO inhibitors.
accept: inhibited MAO allows tyramine to enter circulation and release noradrenaline causing severe vasoconstriction
tyramine is not broken down and displaces noradrenaline from sympathetic nerve endings

questions.q: Which interaction occurs when ethanol is consumed by a patient taking disulfiram, metronidazole, or chlorpropamide?
options: Complete suppression of alcohol intoxication with zero symptoms
Rapid conversion of ethanol into non-toxic acetate without flushing
Direct blockade of muscarinic receptors causing dry mouth only
Disulfiram-like reaction: inhibition of aldehyde dehydrogenase causes acetaldehyde accumulation, resulting in flushing, throbbing headache, nausea, vomiting, and hypotension
questions.explain: Aldehyde dehydrogenase normally oxidizes acetaldehyde to acetic acid; its inhibition causes acetaldehyde buildup and unpleasant systemic symptoms that deter alcohol intake.

open.q: Describe the disulfiram-ethanol reaction and name the enzyme inhibited.
accept: inhibition of aldehyde dehydrogenase causes acetaldehyde accumulation with flushing headache nausea vomiting and hypotension
aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibition leading to acetaldehyde buildup

questions.q: How does co-administration of non-selective beta-blockers (such as propranolol) with insulin or sulfonylureas affect a diabetic patient?
options: They mask sympathetic warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia (tachycardia, tremor) and can prolong hypoglycaemia by inhibiting beta-2-mediated glycogenolysis
They completely cure type 1 diabetes by regenerating pancreatic beta cells
They accelerate renal excretion of insulin within 15 minutes
They prevent glucose absorption across the intestinal brush border
questions.explain: Beta-blockers blunt tremor and palpitations (though sweating, mediated by sympathetic cholinergic fibers, usually persists) and impair beta-2-driven hepatic glycogenolysis and recovery from low blood sugar.

open.q: Explain two hazards of combining non-selective beta-blockers with insulin or sulfonylureas in diabetic patients.
accept: mask tachycardia and tremor of hypoglycaemia and impair glycogenolysis delaying recovery
blunt sympathetic warning signs and inhibit beta-2 glycogenolysis

questions.q: Which drug interaction is caused by co-administering a macrolide antibiotic (such as erythromycin or clarithromycin) with a statin metabolized by CYP3A4 (such as simvastatin)?
options: Rapid breakdown of simvastatin into inactive metabolites
Inhibition of CYP3A4 increases simvastatin plasma levels, raising the risk of myopathy and rhabdomyolysis
Enhanced intestinal absorption of dietary vitamin K
questions.explain: Erythromycin and clarithromycin inhibit CYP3A4, elevating plasma simvastatin concentrations and increasing the risk of skeletal muscle injury (myalgia, myositis, rhabdomyolysis).

open.q: Explain why combining clarithromycin or erythromycin with simvastatin increases the risk of myopathy or rhabdomyolysis.
accept: CYP3A4 inhibition raises simvastatin levels increasing muscle toxicity risk
inhibition of simvastatin metabolism by macrolides

questions.q: Which herbal supplement is a well-known inducer of CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein that lowers plasma concentrations of cyclosporine, tacrolimus, warfarin, and HIV protease inhibitors?
questions.explain: St John's wort induces CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, potentially causing organ transplant rejection, treatment failure, or unplanned pregnancy.

open.q: Name the herbal remedy that induces CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein and reduces levels of cyclosporine and oral contraceptives.

questions.q: Why does combining aspirin or other NSAIDs with warfarin increase bleeding risk through both pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic mechanisms?
options: Aspirin stimulates hepatic synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X
NSAIDs increase vitamin K absorption in the ileum
NSAIDs inhibit platelet aggregation via COX-1 blockade, can irritate gastric mucosa, and may displace warfarin from albumin or inhibit its metabolism
questions.explain: Impairing primary haemostasis (platelets) and mucosal integrity while anticoagulating via vitamin K epoxide reductase inhibition creates a high risk of gastrointestinal and systemic bleeding.

open.q: Give two reasons why co-administering an NSAID with warfarin increases bleeding risk.
accept: antiplatelet effect from COX inhibition and gastric mucosal irritation plus protein binding or metabolic effects
inhibits platelet aggregation and increases GI bleeding risk

questions.q: How is 'drug tolerance' defined in pharmacology?
options: A decrease in response to a given dose of a drug after repeated administration, requiring a larger dose to achieve the same effect
An allergic rash appearing after the first dose of an antibiotic
Complete elimination of a drug from the body within 1 hour
A genetic mutation preventing drug metabolism
questions.explain: Tolerance means a progressively larger dose is needed to produce the same magnitude of effect that was originally produced by a smaller dose.

open.q: Define drug tolerance.
accept: diminished effect on repeated administration requiring a higher dose for the same response

questions.q: What is 'cross-tolerance'?
options: Tolerance developing to a drug only when taken with food
Tolerance to one drug conferring reduced sensitivity to another drug, usually within the same pharmacological class or acting via a similar mechanism
Tolerance that occurs exclusively in elderly patients
A condition where a drug becomes more potent every day
questions.explain: Cross-tolerance occurs among drugs sharing common pathways—for example, tolerance to morphine confers cross-tolerance to heroin or pethidine, and chronic alcohol users show cross-tolerance to benzodiazepines or barbiturates.

open.q: Define cross-tolerance and give one example.
accept: tolerance to one drug reducing response to another drug of a similar class such as morphine and heroin or alcohol and benzodiazepines
shared tolerance between drugs acting on common mechanisms

questions.q: What is 'physical dependence'?
options: An inability to stop taking a drug because of craving alone without any physiological symptoms
An altered physiological state produced by repeated drug administration that results in a characteristic withdrawal (abstinence) syndrome when the drug is stopped or antagonized
A permanent structural deformity of a limb
A preference for intravenous over oral tablets
questions.explain: Physical dependence is neuroadaptation to chronic drug exposure such that abrupt cessation or antagonist administration (e.g., naloxone in opioid dependence) precipitates a characteristic withdrawal syndrome.

open.q: Define physical drug dependence.
accept: neuroadapted physiological state that produces withdrawal symptoms when the drug is stopped or antagonized
state where cessation or an antagonist triggers an abstinence syndrome

questions.q: What is 'psychological dependence' (addiction/substance use disorder behavior)?
options: Slowing of glomerular filtration rate after chronic therapy
Development of a skin rash upon sun exposure
A compulsive drive or craving to seek and take a drug for its rewarding, pleasurable, or relief-producing effects despite harmful consequences
questions.explain: Psychological dependence involves reward-circuit reinforcement, craving, loss of control over drug use, and continued use despite adverse medical, social, or legal consequences.

open.q: Define psychological dependence in substance use.
accept: compulsive craving and drug-seeking behavior for reward or relief despite harm
emotional or psychological drive to keep taking a drug

questions.q: Which brain pathway and neurotransmitter are central to the acute rewarding and reinforcing effects of most addictive drugs (such as opioids, stimulants, nicotine, and alcohol)?
options: The mesolimbic dopaminergic pathway projecting from the ventral tegmental area (VTA) to the nucleus accumbens
questions.explain: Most drugs of abuse increase dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens via the mesolimbic reward circuit originating in the ventral tegmental area.

open.q: Name the main dopaminergic brain reward pathway involved in drug dependence and addiction.

questions.q: Which clinical features characterize acute opioid withdrawal syndrome?
options: Rhinorrhoea, lacrimation, piloerection ('gooseflesh'), yawning, mydriasis, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, anxiety, and tachycardia
Deep coma, pinpoint pupils, and respiratory depression
Complete absence of autonomic or gastrointestinal symptoms
questions.explain: Opioid withdrawal produces a classic sympathetic/autonomic rebound picture—lacrimation, rhinorrhoea, piloerection, dilated pupils, sweating, pilomotor erection, nausea, cramps, and diarrhoea—though it is rarely fatal on its own in healthy adults.

open.q: List three characteristic physical signs or symptoms of opioid withdrawal.
accept: lacrimation rhinorrhoea piloerection mydriasis cramps or diarrhoea
dilated pupils gooseflesh yawning cramps or lacrimation

questions.q: Abrupt withdrawal from which two classes of depressant substances is particularly dangerous because it can cause life-threatening generalized tonic-clonic seizures and delirium tremens?
questions.explain: Chronic alcohol or benzodiazepine use downregulates GABA-A inhibition and upregulates NMDA/glutamate excitation; abrupt cessation can trigger severe autonomic hyperactivity, delirium tremens, and fatal seizures.

open.q: Which two substance classes can cause life-threatening withdrawal seizures or delirium tremens upon abrupt cessation?

questions.q: Which long-acting opioid agonist is widely used in opioid maintenance therapy to prevent withdrawal cravings and reduce illicit opioid use?
questions.explain: Methadone (and buprenorphine) acts at mu-opioid receptors with a long half-life and gradual onset, preventing withdrawal symptoms and reducing high-risk injection behavior.

open.q: Name a long-acting opioid used in maintenance therapy for opioid dependence.

questions.q: Which opioid antagonist is used to prevent relapse in abstinent individuals with opioid use disorder (and also for alcohol use disorder)?
questions.explain: Naltrexone is a long-acting oral or depot opioid receptor antagonist that blocks euphoric effects of opioids and reduces alcohol craving.

open.q: Which oral opioid antagonist is used to support relapse prevention in opioid or alcohol dependence?

questions.q: Which drug is a selective competitive antagonist at benzodiazepine binding sites on GABA-A receptors used to reverse benzodiazepine overdose or excessive sedation?
questions.explain: Flumazenil competitively antagonizes the benzodiazepine site on GABA-A receptors, reversing sedation, though it can precipitate seizures in benzodiazepine-dependent patients or mixed tricyclic overdoses.

open.q: Name the specific antagonist used to reverse benzodiazepine-induced sedation.

questions.q: Why should routine flumazenil administration be avoided in a patient with suspected mixed overdose of benzodiazepines and tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) or in chronic benzodiazepine dependence?
options: Flumazenil causes severe hyperglycaemia within 2 minutes
Reversing GABA-A enhancement can unmask severe tricyclic-induced seizures or arrhythmias and precipitate acute benzodiazepine withdrawal
Flumazenil converts benzodiazepines into toxic cyanide
Flumazenil blocks renal filtration of glucose
questions.explain: Benzodiazepines provide anticonvulsant protection against TCA toxicity; antagonizing them with flumazenil can trigger refractory seizures and severe withdrawal in dependent patients.

open.q: Why is flumazenil risky in patients who are chronically dependent on benzodiazepines or have co-ingested tricyclic antidepressants?
accept: can precipitate seizures and acute withdrawal
unmasks seizures or triggers withdrawal symptoms

questions.q: Which specific antidote is administered for paracetamol (acetaminophen) overdose to replenish hepatic glutathione and detoxify NAPQI?
questions.explain: N-acetylcysteine serves as a glutathione precursor (providing cysteine) and directly conjugates NAPQI, preventing or limiting centrilobular hepatic necrosis when given early.

open.q: Name the specific antidote used to treat paracetamol poisoning.

questions.q: Which specific antidote reverses excessive anticoagulation and bleeding caused by unfractionated heparin?
questions.explain: Protamine sulfate is a strongly basic polypeptide that binds tightly to acidic heparin via ionic attraction to form a stable, inactive complex.

open.q: Name the antidote used to neutralize unfractionated heparin.

questions.q: Which agent is used to reverse warfarin-induced coagulopathy (alongside prothrombin complex concentrate or fresh frozen plasma in major bleeding)?
questions.explain: Warfarin inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase (VKORC1), blocking gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X; vitamin K1 restores cofactor synthesis (taking several hours).

open.q: Which vitamin is given to reverse the anticoagulant effect of warfarin?

questions.q: Which two drugs are combined in the treatment of organophosphate insecticide poisoning (one to block muscarinic effects and one to reactivate phosphorylated acetylcholinesterase before 'aging')?
options: Digoxin immune Fab and calcium gluconate
questions.explain: Atropine antagonizes muscarinic acetylcholine excess (bronchorrhoea, bronchospasm, bradycardia, miosis), while oximes like pralidoxime regenerate active acetylcholinesterase if given before irreversible aging.

open.q: Name the two main antidotes used together in organophosphate poisoning.

questions.q: In organophosphate poisoning, why does pralidoxime fail to restore acetylcholinesterase activity if administered too late after exposure?
options: Pralidoxime is destroyed by gastric acid
Pralidoxime cannot cross the glomerular membrane
The phosphorylated enzyme undergoes 'aging' (dealkylation), becoming resistant to oxime-mediated reactivation
Organophosphates permanently delete the acetylcholinesterase gene
questions.explain: Once the phosphoryl-enzyme complex loses an alkyl group ('aging'), the bond becomes too strong for pralidoxime to cleave, making early administration crucial.

open.q: What biochemical process limits the effectiveness of pralidoxime when treatment of organophosphate poisoning is delayed?
accept: dealkylation or aging of the inhibited cholinesterase

questions.q: Which antidote is used in beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker poisoning when refractory hypotension and myocardial depression fail to respond to standard vasopressors?
options: High-dose insulin euglycaemic therapy (and/or glucagon for beta-blockers)
questions.explain: High-dose insulin improves myocardial calcium handling and carbohydrate metabolism in severe beta-blocker and calcium channel blocker toxicity, while glucagon stimulates cardiac cAMP via a non-beta-adrenergic receptor.

open.q: Name an antidote or specialized therapy used for severe beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker overdose.

questions.q: Which antidote is used for methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning because it has a much higher affinity for alcohol dehydrogenase than methanol or ethylene glycol?
questions.explain: Blocking alcohol dehydrogenase prevents formation of toxic formic acid (from methanol, causing blindness and metabolic acidosis) and glycolic/oxalic acid (from ethylene glycol, causing renal failure and acidosis).

open.q: Name the preferred alcohol dehydrogenase inhibitor used to treat methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning.

questions.q: Which heavy metal chelator is used in severe lead poisoning (often with dimercaprol in encephalopathy)?
questions.explain: Calcium disodium edetate (EDTA) and oral succimer (DMSA) chelate lead to form water-soluble complexes excreted in urine; CaNa2EDTA is used rather than disodium EDTA to avoid fatal hypocalcaemia.

open.q: Name a chelating agent used to treat lead poisoning.

questions.q: Why must calcium disodium edetate (CaNa2EDTA) rather than disodium edetate (Na2EDTA) be used to chelate lead?
options: Disodium EDTA is insoluble in water
Calcium disodium EDTA blocks absorption of lead in the colon
Disodium EDTA binds plasma calcium and can cause fatal hypocalcaemia and tetany
Calcium disodium EDTA increases blood glucose levels
questions.explain: Na2EDTA chelates free calcium ions in plasma, risking severe hypocalcaemia, whereas CaNa2EDTA exchanges its calcium for lead without depleting circulating calcium.

open.q: Explain why calcium disodium EDTA is used for lead chelation instead of disodium EDTA.
accept: disodium EDTA binds serum calcium causing dangerous hypocalcaemia

questions.q: Which chelating agent is used to treat Wilson's disease (hepatolenticular copper overload)?
questions.explain: Penicillamine and trientine chelate copper and promote its urinary excretion in Wilson's disease, while zinc salts induce intestinal metallothionein to block copper absorption.

open.q: Name a copper-chelating drug used in the management of Wilson's disease.

questions.q: Which antidote is used for cyanide poisoning (alongside supportive care and thiosulfate)?
questions.explain: Cyanide binds cytochrome oxidase and halts cellular respiration; hydroxocobalamin binds cyanide to form non-toxic cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12), while nitrites form methaemoglobin to bind cyanide and thiosulfate donates sulfur to form thiocyanate.

open.q: Name an antidote used in acute cyanide poisoning.

questions.q: Which reducing agent is administered intravenously to treat drug-induced methaemoglobinaemia (such as from dapsone, nitrates, or benzocaine)?
questions.explain: Methylene blue is reduced to leukomethylene blue via NADPH-dependent reductase, which donates electrons to reduce ferric iron (Fe3+) in methaemoglobin back to ferrous iron (Fe2+) capable of carrying oxygen.

open.q: Name the antidote used to treat clinically significant drug-induced methaemoglobinaemia.

questions.q: Why can methylene blue be ineffective or even worsen haemolysis when used to treat methaemoglobinaemia in a patient with G6PD deficiency?
options: Methylene blue blocks oxygen binding to normal haemoglobin irreversibly
Methylene blue accelerates renal excretion of glucose
Methylene blue requires NADPH generated via G6PD to act and can induce oxidative haemolysis in G6PD-deficient red blood cells
Methylene blue increases conversion of methaemoglobin into carboxyhaemoglobin
questions.explain: Reduction of methylene blue depends on NADPH from the G6PD pathway; in G6PD deficiency, NADPH is limited and methylene blue can act as an oxidant causing haemolysis (ascorbic acid is an alternative).

open.q: Explain why methylene blue can be ineffective and cause haemolysis in patients with G6PD deficiency.
accept: its reduction relies on NADPH from G6PD and it can trigger oxidative haemolysis in G6PD deficiency
depends on NADPH and may cause haemolysis in G6PD-deficient erythrocytes

questions.q: Which specific immunotherapeutic agent is used to reverse life-threatening digoxin toxicity (such as ventricular arrhythmias or severe hyperkalaemia)?
questions.explain: Digoxin immune Fab binds free and tissue-bound digoxin with high affinity, allowing rapid renal clearance of the Fab-digoxin complex and reversing toxicity.

open.q: Name the specific antidote used for severe digoxin poisoning.

questions.q: Which agent is used to rescue normal cells after high-dose methotrexate therapy by bypassing dihydrofolate reductase inhibition?
questions.explain: Methotrexate inhibits dihydrofolate reductase; leucovorin (5-formyltetrahydrofolate) supplies reduced folate directly to rescue host cells without requiring dihydrofolate reductase.

open.q: Name the reduced folate used as 'rescue' therapy after high-dose methotrexate.

questions.q: Which adverse effect is a classic Type A (pharmacological) reaction to angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors such as captopril or enalapril?
options: Dry, non-productive cough (due to accumulation of bradykinin and substance P)
questions.explain: ACE also degrades bradykinin and substance P; their accumulation sensitizes airway sensory C-fibers, causing a persistent dry cough that resolves after stopping the ACE inhibitor.

open.q: Name a common cough associated with ACE inhibitors and state the endogenous peptide involved.
accept: persistent dry cough from bradykinin or substance P accumulation

questions.q: Which serious, potentially fatal adverse effect of ACE inhibitors and ARBs involves swelling of the lips, tongue, face, or upper airway and requires immediate airway protection and drug discontinuation?
questions.explain: Bradykinin-mediated vasodilation and increased vascular permeability can cause angioedema of the tongue, glottis, or larynx; adrenaline is used if airway compromise threatens life, and ACE inhibitors are permanently avoided.

open.q: Name the potentially life-threatening airway-swelling adverse effect associated with ACE inhibitors.

questions.q: Which drug is classically associated with gingival hyperplasia (overgrowth of gum tissue) and hirsutism during long-term therapy?
questions.explain: Chronic phenytoin therapy can cause gingival overgrowth (fibrous hyperplasia), hirsutism, coarsening of facial features, and megaloblastic anaemia or osteomalacia.

open.q: Name the anticonvulsant drug classically associated with gingival hyperplasia.

questions.q: Which antimicrobial class carries a boxed warning for tendinopathy and tendon rupture (especially the Achilles tendon), peripheral neuropathy, and CNS effects?
questions.explain: Fluoroquinolones can damage tendon collagen/fibroblasts—risk is higher in older adults, patients on corticosteroids, and renal impairment—and are generally avoided in children unless clearly indicated.

open.q: Which class of antibiotics is associated with Achilles tendinitis and tendon rupture?

questions.q: Which drug is classically associated with a 'red man' (infusion-related histamine release) reaction if infused too rapidly intravenously?
questions.explain: Rapid IV infusion of vancomycin directly degranulates mast cells and basophils independently of IgE, causing flushing, erythema of the face and upper torso, and hypotension; prevented by slow infusion and antihistamines.

open.q: Name the glycopeptide antibiotic that causes an infusion-related flushing reaction ('red man syndrome') if infused too fast.

questions.q: Which drug is associated with 'grey-blue' or 'slate-grey' skin pigmentation, corneal deposits, and phototoxicity, and is a classic cause of drug-induced lupus?
questions.explain: Long-term minocycline can cause blue-grey skin/mucosal pigmentation, vestibular toxicity, and autoimmune syndromes including drug-induced lupus and autoimmune hepatitis.

open.q: Name the tetracycline derivative associated with blue-grey skin pigmentation and drug-induced lupus.

questions.q: Which drug requires regular ophthalmological monitoring (visual fields and retinal imaging) during long-term therapy because of irreversible retinopathy?
questions.explain: Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine bind melanin in the retinal pigment epithelium; prolonged high-dose use can cause bull's-eye maculopathy and irreversible visual loss.

open.q: Name the antimalarial/immunomodulatory drug that requires retinal monitoring due to risk of retinopathy.

questions.q: Which psychotropic drug has a narrow therapeutic window and causes tremor, polyuria/polydipsia (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), hypothyroidism, and teratogenic Ebstein anomaly in pregnancy?
questions.explain: Lithium interferes with ADH-mediated water reabsorption in the collecting duct (nephrogenic diabetes insipidus), inhibits thyroid hormone release, and crosses the placenta.

open.q: Name the mood stabilizer associated with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, hypothyroidism, tremor, and Ebstein anomaly.

questions.q: Which antipsychotic drug carries a significant risk of agranulocytosis (requiring regular absolute neutrophil count monitoring) as well as myocarditis and metabolic syndrome?
questions.explain: Clozapine is reserved for treatment-resistant schizophrenia because of potentially fatal agranulocytosis (severe neutropenia), myocarditis, and seizures, requiring mandatory blood count monitoring.

open.q: Which atypical antipsychotic requires routine white blood cell/neutrophil monitoring due to the risk of agranulocytosis?

questions.q: Which endocrine/metabolic adverse effect is characteristic of prolonged systemic corticosteroid therapy?
options: Primary hyperaldosteronism with hypokalemic alkalosis and hypotension
Iatrogenic Cushing syndrome, adrenal suppression (HPA axis suppression), osteoporosis, hyperglycaemia, and increased susceptibility to infection
questions.explain: Exogenous glucocorticoids cause Cushingoid features, catabolic bone loss/osteoporosis, insulin resistance/hyperglycaemia, immunosuppression, and suppression of endogenous ACTH/cortisol.

open.q: State three characteristic adverse effects of prolonged systemic corticosteroid therapy.
accept: Cushingoid features adrenal suppression osteoporosis hyperglycaemia or infection risk

questions.q: Why must chronic systemic corticosteroid therapy be tapered gradually rather than stopped abruptly?
options: Abrupt stopping causes immediate drug accumulation in adipose tissue
Corticosteroids are excreted only through sweat glands
Exogenous steroids suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, so sudden withdrawal can precipitate acute adrenal crisis (hypotension, shock, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia)
questions.explain: Prolonged steroid exposure inhibits CRH and ACTH secretion and causes adrenocortical atrophy; tapering allows endogenous HPA axis recovery to prevent Addisonian crisis.

open.q: Explain why prolonged systemic corticosteroid therapy must be tapered gradually rather than discontinued abruptly.
accept: prevents acute adrenal crisis due to suppressed HPA axis and adrenocortical atrophy
allows recovery of suppressed hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis

questions.q: Which adverse effect is associated with prolonged use of proton pump inhibitors (such as omeprazole) due to chronic hypochlorhydria and altered calcium/mineral absorption?
options: Increased risk of bone fractures, hypomagnesaemia, Clostridium difficile infection, and vitamin B12 malabsorption
questions.explain: Sustained gastric acid suppression reduces calcium/B12 absorption and impairs the gastric acid barrier against enteric pathogens like Clostridioides difficile.

open.q: Name two adverse effects associated with long-term proton pump inhibitor therapy.
accept: fracture risk hypomagnesaemia Clostridioides difficile infection or B12 deficiency

questions.q: Which rare but life-threatening metabolic complication is associated with metformin accumulation, especially in patients with severe renal impairment, hypoxia, or sepsis?
questions.explain: Metformin inhibits mitochondrial complex I and alters hepatic lactate clearance; when renal excretion falls or tissue hypoxia increases lactate production, lactic acidosis can develop.

open.q: Name the serious metabolic complication linked to metformin accumulation in renal or hypoxic states.

questions.q: Which serious arrhythmia risk is shared by several drugs that prolong the QT interval on the electrocardiogram (such as certain antiarrhythmics, macrolides, fluoroquinolones, and antipsychotics)?
options: Complete heart block with narrow QRS
questions.explain: Prolongation of ventricular repolarization (delayed IKr potassium current and prolonged QTc) predisposes to early afterdepolarizations and torsades de pointes, which can degenerate into ventricular fibrillation.

open.q: Name the polymorphic ventricular tachycardia arrhythmia triggered by drug-induced QT interval prolongation.

questions.q: What does 'pharmaceutical incompatibility' mean in clinical practice?
options: An interaction occurring at postsynaptic dopamine receptors
Induction of hepatic CYP2C9 by phenobarbital
Physicochemical interaction occurring outside the body (e.g., precipitation, inactivation, or turbidity when two drugs are mixed in the same syringe or IV fluid)
Genetic variation in NAT2 acetylation rate
questions.explain: Pharmaceutical incompatibility happens before administration—for example, mixing alkaline phenytoin with acidic dextrose solutions causing precipitation, or mixing beta-lactams with aminoglycosides in the same IV bag.

open.q: Define pharmaceutical incompatibility and give an example.
accept: in vitro physicochemical interaction such as precipitation or inactivation when drugs are mixed in IV fluids
physical or chemical incompatibility outside the body before administration

questions.q: How does cholestyramine reduce the absorption and therapeutic effect of co-administered oral warfarin, digoxin, or levothyroxine if taken at the same time?
options: It stimulates rapid hepatic glucuronidation of those drugs
It increases renal tubular secretion of those drugs
It dilates splanchnic arterioles to wash drugs away
It binds these drugs non-specifically in the intestinal lumen and impairs their gastrointestinal absorption
questions.explain: Bile acid resins can adsorb acidic or lipophilic drugs in the gut; separating dosing times (e.g., taking other drugs 1 hour before or 4 hours after cholestyramine) reduces this interaction.

open.q: How does cholestyramine interfere with the oral absorption of drugs like warfarin or levothyroxine?
accept: binds them in the gut lumen reducing absorption

questions.q: Why does co-administration of cimetidine (unlike famotidine) have a higher potential for pharmacokinetic drug interactions?
options: Cimetidine inhibits hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes (such as CYP1A2, CYP2D6, CYP3A4), whereas famotidine has minimal effect on CYP enzymes
Cimetidine is a potent inducer of P-glycoprotein
Cimetidine irreversibly binds to serum albumin
Cimetidine blocks renal glomerular filtration completely
questions.explain: Cimetidine inhibits CYP enzymes and renal organic cation transport, raising levels of drugs like theophylline, warfarin, and phenytoin, whereas famotidine largely avoids CYP inhibition.

open.q: Why does cimetidine cause more CYP-mediated drug interactions than famotidine?
accept: cimetidine inhibits hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes while famotidine does not significantly inhibit them

questions.q: What happens when a patient taking a non-selective beta-blocker (such as propranolol) is given adrenaline for acute anaphylaxis or hypotension?
options: Beta-2 vasodilation is enhanced without any rise in blood pressure
Beta-2-mediated vasodilation is blocked while alpha-1-mediated vasoconstriction persists unopposed, which can cause a sharp rise in blood pressure and reflex bradycardia
Adrenaline is completely inactivated by beta-blockers in plasma
Heart rate rises to over 220 bpm immediately
questions.explain: Blocking beta-2 receptors removes adrenaline's vasodilatory counterbalance in skeletal muscle beds, leaving unopposed alpha-1 vasoconstriction and risking hypertension and reflex vagal bradycardia.

open.q: Explain the hemodynamic effect of unopposed alpha-adrenergic stimulation when adrenaline is given to someone on a non-selective beta-blocker.
accept: alpha-1 vasoconstriction occurs without beta-2 vasodilation causing hypertension and reflex bradycardia

questions.q: What is 'pharmacodynamic (cellular) tolerance'?
options: Faster hepatic metabolism of a drug after repeated dosing
Reduced drug absorption across the intestinal mucosa
Adaptive changes at the receptor or intracellular signaling level (such as receptor desensitization or downregulation) despite unchanged drug concentrations at the target
Increased renal excretion of unchanged drug
questions.explain: Pharmacodynamic tolerance reflects cellular/receptor adaptation (e.g., opioid receptor desensitization and adenylate cyclase upregulation), whereas dispositional (metabolic) tolerance reflects faster clearance (e.g., enzyme induction).

open.q: Define pharmacodynamic tolerance and contrast it briefly with metabolic tolerance.
accept: reduced cellular or receptor responsiveness despite constant drug levels whereas metabolic tolerance involves faster drug clearance
receptor or intracellular adaptation rather than faster elimination

questions.q: What is 'dispositional (metabolic) tolerance'?
options: Downregulation of postsynaptic receptors in the striatum
Formation of IgE antibodies against a drug
Development of a severe skin rash
Decreased drug concentration at the site of action upon repeated dosing, commonly due to hepatic enzyme induction (autoinduction)
questions.explain: Repeated exposure to an enzyme inducer (such as carbamazepine or phenobarbital) increases metabolic enzyme synthesis, accelerating clearance and lowering plasma levels for a given dose.

open.q: Define dispositional (metabolic) tolerance.
accept: reduced drug levels on repeated dosing due to increased elimination or enzyme induction
faster clearance or metabolism after repeated exposure

questions.q: Why is spontaneous adverse drug reaction reporting ('pharmacovigilance') essential even after a drug completes Phase III clinical trials?
options: Pre-marketing trials involve relatively limited sample sizes and selected patients, so rare ADRs (<1 in 1,000 to 1 in 10,000), delayed effects, and real-world interactions may not be detected until wider use
Phase III trials never test drug safety in any humans
Drugs are never tested for toxicity before clinical approval
Post-marketing reporting is only used to set retail prices
questions.explain: Clinical trials cannot capture every rare idiosyncratic reaction, long-term toxicity, or interaction in multimorbid populations before licensing, making post-marketing surveillance vital.

open.q: Explain why post-marketing adverse drug reaction reporting is necessary despite pre-approval clinical trials.
accept: trials have limited sample sizes and selected patients so rare delayed or real-world ADRs emerge during broader clinical use
detects rare delayed and real-world adverse effects not seen in smaller pre-marketing trials

questions.q: Why are older adults (geriatric patients) more vulnerable to adverse drug reactions than young adults?
options: They have markedly increased glomerular filtration rate and hepatic blood flow
Age-related decline in renal and hepatic clearance, altered body composition (increased fat, decreased lean mass/total body water), polypharmacy, and altered pharmacodynamic sensitivity
They absorb zero drugs from the gastrointestinal tract
questions.explain: Reduced GFR, lower hepatic clearance, changes in volume of distribution, multimorbidity, and polypharmacy increase drug accumulation and ADR risk in older adults ('start low, go slow').

open.q: Give two reasons why elderly patients have a higher risk of adverse drug reactions.
accept: reduced renal or hepatic clearance polypharmacy altered body composition or increased sensitivity

questions.q: Which antimicrobial drug is associated with disulfiram-like reactions when combined with alcohol, peripheral neuropathy, and metallic taste?
questions.explain: Metronidazole causes a metallic taste, can cause peripheral neuropathy with prolonged or high doses, and can trigger disulfiram-like flushing/nausea with alcohol.

open.q: Name the nitroimidazole antimicrobial associated with a metallic taste, disulfiram-like alcohol reaction, and peripheral neuropathy.

questions.q: Which drug-induced complication is associated with prolonged use of unfractionated heparin or low-molecular-weight heparin and presents with a falling platelet count and paradoxical thrombosis?
questions.explain: HIT is an immune-mediated disorder (antibodies against platelet factor 4-heparin complexes) that activates platelets and causes venous and arterial thrombosis despite low platelet counts, requiring cessation of heparin and a non-heparin anticoagulant.

open.q: Name the immune-mediated complication of heparin therapy characterized by thrombocytopenia and paradoxical thrombosis.

questions.q: Which specific reversing agent is used to rapidly neutralize dabigatran (a direct thrombin inhibitor) in life-threatening bleeding or emergency surgery?
questions.explain: Idarucizumab is a humanized monoclonal antibody fragment that binds dabigatran with very high affinity to rapidly reverse its anticoagulant effect.

open.q: Name the specific reversal agent for dabigatran.

questions.q: What is the most important immediate clinical step when a serious adverse drug reaction (such as drug rash with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, or anaphylaxis) is suspected?
options: Double the dose to see if tolerance develops
Promptly discontinue the suspected causative drug (and treat acute emergencies such as anaphylaxis immediately)
Wait two weeks without changing therapy to observe if symptoms resolve spontaneously
Switch to another drug of the exact same chemical class with known cross-reactivity
questions.explain: Early recognition and prompt withdrawal of the offending drug—paired with immediate resuscitation for emergencies like anaphylaxis—are critical to prevent progression and morbidity.

open.q: State the most important initial management step when a serious adverse drug reaction is suspected.
accept: stop or discontinue the suspected drug promptly
discontinue the offending drug and provide appropriate supportive or emergency care
